title: Magnetotransport experiments on side-contacted topological insulator three-terminal Josephson junctions
authors: Christoph Wassmer, Ella Nikodem, Oliver Breunig, Yongjian Wang, Yoichi Ando, Jakob Schluck
abstract: Multiterminal Josephson junctions have recently attracted substantial attention. The ability to study Andreev bound states in a multi-phase parameter space opens up exciting avenues for generating topologically non-trivial phases in superconducting devices. A particularly interesting case is the trijunction based on a topological insulator (TI), which is predicted to host Majorana zero modes for suitable phase configurations (Fu and Kane, PRL 2008). Here we turn to the platform of the side-contacted TI trijunction and present experimental evidence for a multiterminal Josephson effect. We study the transport properties and find typical features of a two-dimensional critical current contour (CCC) as well as bias regimes in which only a single junction remains dissipationless. We pay particular attention to these features and study the effects of magnetic fields on single junctions within the trijunction, where, depending on the field direction, the supercurrents show Fraunhofer patterns, SQUID oscillations, or a monotonic decay. We find good agreement with semiclassical simulations for a single TI junction that take into account the top and bottom surface states. We observe pronounced non-convex shape deformations of the CCC under perpendicular magnetic fields that reflect the flux buildup in the loop formed by our trijunctions and provide a simple model sufficient to explain the observed effect. Our results provide the foundations for future studies of Majorana zero modes on this platform.
summary: This work experimentally characterizes the magnetotransport of a three-terminal Josephson junction fabricated on a topological insulator. By measuring the critical current contours and single-junction responses under applied magnetic fields, the authors confirm the device's superconducting nature. The results provide a foundational platform for future research aiming to observe Majorana zero modes.
main_problem: The study investigates the magnetotransport properties of a three-terminal Josephson junction built on a topological insulator (TI) to characterize its superconducting state and search for signatures of Majorana zero modes (MZMs).
main_result: The experiment successfully measured characteristic trijunction transport features, including the Critical Current Contour (CCC) deformation under magnetic fields, and confirmed the single-junction response using semiclassical models.
method: Transport measurements were performed using lock-in techniques on the TI junction, varying bias currents and applying external magnetic fields in different orientations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a side-contacted TI trijunction connected to superconducting leads. The analysis employs the Resistively Shunted Junction (RCSJ) model and semiclassical trajectory simulations to interpret the measured supercurrents.
key_observables: Differential resistance maps (dV/dI), Critical Current Contours (CCC), Fraunhofer interference patterns, and SQUID oscillations.
important_parameters: Applied magnetic fields ($B_{\perp}, B_{\parallel}$), bias currents ($I_1, I_2$), and junction geometry parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed transport features can be modeled by considering the topological surface states and that the collective behavior can be understood by summing individual junction responses.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images, 3D schematics, 2D bias maps illustrating transport regimes (A-E), and detailed plots showing the magnetic field dependence of the critical current for isolated junctions (Fraunhofer, SQUID).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general trijunction transport features (CCC, resistive regimes) to isolating the response of individual junctions under various magnetic field orientations, and finally comparing these measurements against semiclassical simulations.
why_interesting: The study provides experimental validation of superconducting phenomena in topological materials, which is crucial for realizing topological quantum computing elements, bridging condensed matter physics with quantum information.

FIG. 4. Three-terminal response of device 2 to small B⊥, showing a cyclic deformation of the CCC. While the indi- vidual critical currents of the junctions remain largely unaf- fected, an imposed phase condition between terminals leads to deformations of the CCC. (a) Zero-field bias map. (b) The deformation sets in on the left half of the contour, extends to the right half (c), and is strongest at 800 µT (d), where the contour becomes non-convex and diamond-shaped. It then relaxes, again first on the left half (e). (f) At 1900 µT, the CCC is restored in a shape similar to, but smaller than, the zero-field case, resulting from an overall reduced Ic.
